utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was -- is not aware of any preliminaries to be raised. Therefore, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time and say something about P2508 which is MFI'd. It was tendered with Witness Riedlmayer. On the 3rd of December of this year, the Chamber asked the Prosecution to redact P2508, which is a lengthy document covering more than 450 pages. On the 6th of December, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence that it had redacted the document to portions referred to by Witness Riedlmayer and Okun. And the Prosecution has uploaded the redacted version of P2508 under 65 ter number 02382A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Chamber would like to hear from the Defence what their position is on the admission of the now redacted or the reduced -- the document which is reduced in size. Could we hear later from you today, Mr. Lukic? Yes. Good morning, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I have to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examination by Mr. Ivetic [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of your direct examination, at transcript page 20228, you were shown 65 ter number 03975, a copy of your curriculum vitae. You commented that you were surprised that the Prosecution was using that particular version as it had been subsequently corrected by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please call up 65 ter number 11462 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on the screen is the version of your curriculum vitae which was also disclosed to us by the Prosecution and which I reviewed to prepare for your examination. Is this, in fact, a more recent and accurate CV than the one we looked at last week, which was 65 ter number 03975?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to make two comments. It is indeed -- I mean, this version is accurate for what my educational background is concerned, but it does -- still doesn't include my currently professional occupations; i.e., the position I have held since leaving the ICTY in April 2009. If my recollection is correct, in the Hadzic trial, I mean the last trial I testified prior to this trial, a fully correct version of my CV was tendered, but I am not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to focus on the educational portion of this curriculum vitae which you have now indicated is correct. The curriculum vitae which was being used last week by the Prosecution listed some additional degree work from the years 2000 to 2001 at CERIS in Brussels for a masters in international politics, yet that course work is missing from this newer CV. Can you explain for us if you ever finished that second degree and why that information is not to be located on this curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not finish that additional -- those additional studies, and this is largely due to my move to the ICTY in June 2001. I had hoped that during the initial years of my work in ICTY I had been in a position to finish that, but I had no time. And this is why, obviously -- I mean, it doesn't make much sense to include unfinished studies in a CV. This is why in a later version of my CV, those studies were not included.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now in this version just above the section relating to education, in the personal data we have a notation of your military rank --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- as a commandant, in parenthesis (OF-3), end parenthesis. And I wanted to ask you to explain for us what the designation OF-3 means here in relation to your rank?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the Belgian military for officers we have a rank between captain and major and that rank is called commandant or sometimes captain commandant, not to be confounded with the French rank of commandant which is the same as a major, or, also, I think, in the Irish military the rank of commandant corresponds with major. However, in -- when using NATO equivalents, NATO uses OF and then various digits to describe the rank level. In NATO equivalent, the rank of captain-commandant or commandant, as it is used in the Belgian military, corresponds with an OF-3, which is also the acronym used for major, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now with respect to the Belgian military, am I correct that there is a position which is called chief of the defence staff within the Belgian military that is to be staffed according to the establishment by a four-star general as its chief -- as the chief?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us within the Belgian military's rank echelons, how many ranks are between that of a commandant at OF-3 and the four-star general, that is the chief of the defence staff? If I can assist, would it be approximately six or seven rank echelons?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, for maybe -- for the interests of the trial court -- of the Trial Chamber, I'm sorry, I can give you all ranks. The next rank is major; then the one above is lieutenant-colonel; then we have colonel; then we have major-general; I jump brigadier-general because it's only recently that the Belgian military, I mean, if you consider relevant, has designated brigadier-generals, otherwise brigadier-generals were only appointed on a temporary basis for assignments outside the Belgian military; and after the major-general, you have lieutenant-general; and then there is the one four-star. If I am not mistaken, the Belgian king is also a four-star. Maybe that is also of interest for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. And the Belgian king is the commandant of all forces would sit -- would sit above the chief of the defence staff in the hierarchy; isn't that also correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's actually the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just waiting for the translation to catch up with us. Now, in relation to your military career within the Belgian military, and your experience as a commanding officer, is it correct that you served as acting commander of a company consisting of 80 soldiers on a few occasions, but that apart from those instances your top command post was as a platoon commander responsible for 15 subordinate soldiers?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, factually that is correct. But, I mean, I don't like the expression "top command post," because when discussing military careers, I mean, the expression top command post, it's not like a hit parade or something. The command post you have is equivalent to your rank and obviously then to your age. So if I left the military when I was a commandant, it was difficult for me to achieve a more senior command post, because in order to command a battalion, for example, you have to be at least lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I use "top," I mean "most senior," sir, so if there is any confusion about that, please take that into consideration. And apart from the position that you held as acting commander of a company on several occasions, your most senior commandant post as a platoon commander would have involved command over approximately four tanks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. A tank platoon is four tanks, full stop. So it wouldn't make more sense -- it wouldn't make sense to try to command more tanks in one platoon. That is a reason why a platoon has only four tanks, a tank platoon, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now if we can focus again on the most senior position that you did hold, which was as an acting commander of a company. Am I correct that this post was only held by you approximately one or two weeks at a time on several occasions during the course of your military career?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And I -- I mean, this was for shorter time-periods because I replaced the actual commander who was on training courses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you confirm for us that in relation to your command experience, at all times this was service during peacetime; that is, you did not serve in a commander function during any time of war or in a war zone?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you clarify for us that you have never commanded over any artillery unit at any level in the course of your career?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not. I mean, just to -- I think it's important to clarify. As a junior officer in armour, I attended, I think it was a one- or a two-week training in what we call advanced observer; i.e., that you are -- because you are closer to the confrontation line than the artillery commander, and, as you know, artillery uses the concept of indirect fire. I have been trained in adjusting artillery fire on a target. And I have also, I mean, if that can be of assistance, during my military education academy, I attended the optional training of ballistics which actually was very useful for the work I did here as a military analyst in the OTP because it allowed me to understand the concept of how artillery fire functions, the fact that you do not necessarily hit a target because you cover a zone, and the various mathematical and statistical calculations that are involved in that. So I do believe I have an understanding of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that your understanding of command over artillery units and the functioning of artillery weapons is such that you would hold yourself out to be an expert on those topics?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the second time that you raise the issue of expert or not. I mean, my answer will be the same. It's up to the Trial Chamber to decide whether or not I am an expert or not. I just want to add also that when I attended the brigade level staff course, 1996, 1997, obviously that also involved the preparation of artillery orders; i.e., the use of artillery support in a manner that would be the most effective to support the operations offensive or defensive of ground forces, whether those were infantry or artillery, and obviously we also had courses on the international laws of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now how about General Mladic's position as the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS? Do you consider yourself to be able to reliably opine as a military expert as to a military commander holding a position at that echelon level based on your limited command experience within the Belgian military?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, to the extent over the last five pages you want to draw attention to the fact that Mr. Theunens did not gain his knowledge and skills primarily in operational functions, then that is perfectly clear and could have been done in half a page. If there is anything more important, please go to that matter, that issue directly. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this goes to methodology not to his background, as he believed, based upon his experiences --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then go to methodology, Mr. Ivetic, instead of going through 15 people, four tanks, that is all practical experience you are focusing at. And if there is any methodological matter, please put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, based upon your limited command experience within the Belgian military, do you believe, methodologically speaking, that you are able to opine as to General Mladic's position as commander of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, or Mr. Ivetic, also, I believe there is a misunderstanding. The methodology apply -- that I applied for the report is not an aspect of command and control. The methodology consists of reviewing a substantial amount of documents and then to draw -- I mean, to try to identify, first of all, patterns or trends; and then on the basis of those, to try to draw analytical conclusions. We have discussed the methodology in the examination. I believe that on the basis of my educational background, including the additional trainings I attended in UK and the US on the one hand, and on the other hand my professional experience, that I am qualified to draw analytical conclusions on a subject like the role of General Mladic as commander -- excuse me, as deputy commander of the 2nd Military District, and subsequently commander of the 2nd Military District, as well as commander of the VRS Main Staff. And as I mentioned before, it is then up to the Trial Chamber to decide whether or not that experience and the way how I have used that experience and expertise matches the requirements to be considered and accepted as an expert or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can take a look at page 2 in both languages of this curriculum vitae, I want to now switch gears and look at the publications listed. Actually, if we can have the next in B/C/S. I think we have -- one more page in B/C/S. It should be item number 6 on the last part of the CV. There we go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at the publications listed, I want to ask you if apart from these publications listed here, are there any other publications that you have authored about the JNA or the VRS which you feel to be significant which are not identified on this list?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that the list of publications is incomplete because, I mean, I also -- first of all, the reports I wrote for various trials which were then admitted into evidence as expert reports, I listed them here as publications because this is my CV only for court. Obviously these are not publications outside the context of ICTY. I have the impression that this list stops as 2005. I mean, after that there were reports for - I am just trying to check - for the Stanisic-Simatovic case. There was a report for the Hadzic case. There was a report -- I'm -- also for the Seselj case, I don't think it's included. So those are missing. I did a report for Gotovina et al. case, but obviously that was not focused on the JNA but more on the ZNG and the HV. So that is what I can answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also have occasion to draft or author an article on the role of military expertise in the prosecution of trials for international crimes in 2009?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, Your Honours. And that was indeed published outside the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time I would like to look at document 1D1498 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the publication which you authored in 2009 on the role of military expertise in the prosecution and trials for international crimes, you in the introduction, talking about the systemic and/or wide-spread nature of crimes, cite to -- cite twice to a different publication authored by Ms. Carla del Ponte. And I'd like to ask you, methodologically speaking, do you consider it appropriate and professional to cite to the Prosecutor as a sole supporting reference in relation to professional articles that you are authoring on points of relevance?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we don't have the article here and I don't exactly recall for which specific package I cited another publication by Ms. Del Ponte. But in that context, I don't see a problem with that. I mean, in this specific context, I don't see a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now in relation to the article by del Ponte, do you recall the article that you would have reviewed by Ms. Del Ponte from 2006 called: "Investigation and Prosecution of Large-Scale Crimes at the International Level"?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a general impression of what the article states but it's seven years ago, and the last four years I have been focusing on rather different matters, so I couldn't say more about the article. So for the transcript, the last -- during the last four years, I have been focusing on very different matters, so I wouldn't be able to say more about the 2006 article by Mrs. Del Ponte.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One moment. I'm just trying to get this one up and running.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now try again to have 1D1498 up in e-court. And if we can turn to page 3 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the quote I was making reference to is in the first paragraph, the middle of the same, and -- well, actually, the entire first two sentences, the first two footnotes relate to the material that you are citing to Ms. Del Ponte on. They read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the footnotes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There we go. That's probably the best way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection as to what subject matter you would have been relying upon Ms. Del Ponte on for purposes of your professionally written article?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And now I'd like to ask you again, do you consider as someone said to be an expert for this type of -- these type of assertions, for you to have the sole reference being Ms. Carla del Ponte who was the Prosecutor at the Tribunal, from a methodological standpoint?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mean, you can always include more footnotes but I think these -- these statements are very straight-forward and very obvious for anyone who is familiar with this subject matter, so I don't think it would have been of assistance to include more footnotes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now looking at the date of Ms. Del Ponte's article, I believe she was still your boss at the time that she wrote it. Do you know if the assertions made by Ms. Del Ponte in her article are her own opinion or is she relying upon your work as an analyst in making these assertions?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know, Your Honours. And, I mean, in my language the word "boss" would be inappropriate in this context. She was the Prosecutor. I was working in the Office of the Prosecutor. But she was not my direct nor second supervisor. So in my language, pets have bosses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I do see that footnote 1 is supporting a statement which says that: "Serious violations of international humanitarian law in the context of the conflict of the former Yugoslavia often involved co-ordinated action between various enforcement agencies ..." Is there dispute about that? You say there was -- it did not or not often involved such co-ordinated action.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours I -- I an talking about the methodology of an expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it's a one-side view of the facts to present it in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it's not entirely accurate the way it's presented. Co-ordination of the various forces is a tenet of the Prosecution's theory of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think she describes a factual situation. But it often involved, that's one. Second, for footnote 2: "The systemic and/or wide-spread nature of some of the crimes suggests that the actions and operations of these physical perpetrators were planned, co-ordinated, and organised at the highest ... decision-making levels." Is it the position of the Defence that systemic and wide-spread do not suggest, apart from what happened in relation to the charges, that this is not something a prosecutor could use? And the question then, of course, is -- but let me leave it to that. Let's focus not on factual matters. If there is any problem here, what you should demonstrate is that it is inappropriate for what this witness says to rely on the Prosecutor where the Prosecutor describes practical experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then if we can look down further on the page, the end of the second paragraph. I'd like to look at something that Mr. Theunens, I believe, has written that is not related to the Prosecutor. And I believe it's the result of his practical experience, if I'm reading it correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last line of that -- the last sentence in that paragraph, sir, reads as follows: "The evidence presented at various trials at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), however, demonstrates that these paramilitary formations, together with local Serb forces, were supported by the republic of Serbia and the JNA and operated in co-ordination with or under JNA command." And now you are citing two various judgements from the ICTY in relation to this part of your article. Do you consider it methodologically appropriate for a military expert to rely upon holdings of Trial Chambers as to the source for conclusions about command over formations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a distinction between an article and a report that is to be submitted for a trial as an expert report. I do not see a problem in using judgements of the ICTY as references for an article that is for -- of public interest. As you can see from the expert report -- or the report, sorry, that's has been tendered in this case, there are no references to any judgements or what I would call similar secondary or even third sources in -- to substantiate or to support conclusions. I have almost exclusively for this underlying report for this case, based myself on primary sources, i.e., military as well as other documents from the SFRY, FRY, the SRBiH, and the RS. So there is a distinction between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can move to page 5 in e-court of this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the section that is now on the screen, you are talking about the military analyst team or MAT team at the Tribunal. I'd like to look at -- with you at the second paragraph, the first two sentences of the same, which read: "Military analysis or (in-house) military expertise provides investigation and subsequently prosecution cases with the military dimension of integrated events, personalities, organisations, and crimes under scrutiny. In simple terms, military expertise present a picture of who was doing what to whom, when, where, how, and why in the military sense." Does this accurately depict your understanding and belief about the role that you were to fulfil as a military analyst expert within the Office of the Prosecutor at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my job title was intelligence analyst (military), the word "expert" was not part of my job title.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Does this selection that we have just read comport with what you believed your job title was meant to do?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, this is how my former team leader, Mr. Peter Nicholson described the role of military analysis in an article he published in 2003, as the footnote states, and I agree with his view on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you consider Mr. Nicholson to be authoritative on the topic of military analysts and military experts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on military analysis, I do. I mean, I understand that he was selected here, I mean, and he worked on a number of years as a team leader of the military analyst team, so I trust that he was competent to do that job. Now, where I -- my personal view is that an expert should also be an analyst. Obviously, not every analyst is an expert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to 65 ter number 1D1496.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is not in e-court, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment. If we can now again try to have 1D01496 called up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is this the article that we are discussing by your former team leader, Mr. Peter Nicholson, that you cited to in the prior article that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does Your Honours. I cited some of the passages from this article for my own article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now in relation to citing just some of this article in your article, do you agree with everything that has -- do you agree that Mr. Nicholson has written everything in here as accurately and truthfully setting forth the standards for the field of military analysis and military expertise, or is there anything in here that you would disagree with?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not seen this article since 2009, so if Mr. Ivetic would like me to comment on the article, then I would propose that he give me a hard copy, I review it during that break, and then after the break we go into it. And I would also like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention that I have not used Mr. Nicholson's article for the report on the role and authority of the General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, I propose while we wait for the hard copy for you to review at the break, that I could point to the specific items and have you comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could move to page 2 in e-court of this article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the heading of topic 2, Function of Military Analysis. And Mr. Nicholson has written here as follows: "Military analysis provides investigation and subsequently prosecution cases with the military dimension of integrated events, personalities, organisations, and crimes under scrutiny. The analyst will exam de jure and de facto issues relating to crimes, prosecution targets, and events, and will provide analysis from the most preliminary stages of an investigation or assessment, right through to the presentation in court of such analyses by the analyst for the prosecution. She/he provides the ability to monitor, research for, and advise, the prosecutor in the defence phase of a trial." Do you agree that he has accurately described your role here in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand, my role, when, how, what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your role as a military analyst within the Office of the Prosecutor, sir.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a fairly accurately description. Personally, I didn't like the expression "prosecution targets" because I don't see my work as targeting. I see my work as providing military knowledge and background to, as I was employed by the Office of the Prosecutor, to members of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could please move to page 3 of this article in e-court. I would like to focus on the last paragraph of the same, under the heading "Command Responsibility, use of Military Experts."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here Mr. Nicholson states as follows: "The analyst will offer advice in the use or not of an external military expert or experts during the investigative and prosecutorial phase of a case. Such an expert/experts can provide added value to the case by providing advice, and eventually writing a report and giving evidence, in relation to the targeted accused, his/her knowledge and his/her likely command responsibility for events and crimes which have taken place. The expert should be of similar or higher rank than the target/accused, and have had operational experience or similar in order to authenticate and valid the 'expert' label." Do you agree with that which Mr. Nicholson has written here about the qualifications necessary more a military expert?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the views of Mr. Nicholson are obviously very interesting, but it's -- again, its up to the Trial Chamber to decide whether a -- an individual that has been presented as an expert witness - whether it's on the side of the Prosecution or Defence - will indeed be recognised as an expert and his or her evidence accepted as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you agree or disagree with Mr. Nicholson as to what is the standard for a person to be retained as a military expert?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't disagree with him. I think you have to look at the specific situation and the specific nature of the expertise that is required. The article dates from 2003 and then the common practice, as I understand it, in the OTP was to have both an in-house expert whose focus would be on reviewing documents and again identifying patterns and trends among these documents and then present those conclusions to the Trial Chamber during testimony; and secondly, to have also an external expert who would obviously not be tasked with reviewing such significant amounts of documents but where first and foremost the OTP would rely on that person's experience, practical experience in command and control. And this is actually also exactly what I have described my article. So this double approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you tell us exactly where you read in the portion you have drawn our attention to that Mr. Nicholson has written about - and you're referring to ranks and experience - are a qualifications necessary to be a military expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The last line of page 3 and the first half line of page 4, that read: "The expert should be of similar or higher rank than the target accused and have had the operational experience or similar in order to authenticate and validate the expert label."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us where he says that that is a necessary requirement? Is there a possibility, for example, that you could understand this as a strategic approach by the Office of the Prosecution? I do not see the words "this is necessary, otherwise he does not qualify as a expert," because that's what you're putting to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if someone cannot validate the expert label, he is not an expert. That's my reading of the English language used by Mr. Nicholson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Then perhaps the first thing we could ask the witness is whether he agrees with that reading of this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Theunens, with Mr. Ivetic, that Mr. Nicholson here describes the necessary qualifications to be -- to qualify as a military expert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I do not. I mean, as you had clarified. And as I also tried to clarify, Mr. Nicholson is talking about the very specific case of military experts, a very specific type of military experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can look at the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Theunens, I did not -- I have not clarified anything. I have raised a question in relation to the interpretation of the text written by Mr. Nicholson, just to avoid any misunderstanding. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down to the bottom of the page that we have on the screen before us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholson also talks about the use of military experts in an organisational function analysis. And if you read -- I don't think we need to read aloud the two paragraphs involved about this section, but I think you will agree with me that Mr. Nicholson makes the same observations about an expert needing to be -- should be of appropriate rank and/or experience, be of sufficient knowledge, and have had operational experience or similar where appropriate in order to authenticate or validate the expert label. In relation to this type of expert and this type of analysis of an organisation rather than an individual, do you agree with what Mr. Nicholson has included here?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree nor disagree. I mean, there are things in what Mr. Nicholson writes that do make sense. There are others where I think given the fact his article dates from 2003 that maybe now, ten years later, we may draw different conclusions. And again, I have the impression that you paraphrase what Mr. Nicholson writes in a particular way to create, I don't know, some kind of even suspicion where it's all very factual and very simple as I also described my own article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What you do you feel -- if it's so simple, what do you feel would be the appropriate rank and/or experience for an expert to perform the type of analysis that we are talking about here, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what Mr. Nicholson describes is the approach that was applied at the ICTY, say, between 2001 or even before that in, I believe, 2004 and 2005; that is, that we would have at least two military experts. There would be the in-house person who would -- whose first task would be or whose main task would be to review documents, and those would be thousands of documents held by the OTP. This includes also documents provided by the Defence at various trials. And that analyst would apply then the well known methodology of the intelligence cycle in order to identify patterns and trends, which would then lay the foundation for conclusions that would be included in an expert report that would be submitted during the Prosecution phase of the trial. The second category that was used at the time were the so-called external experts, where you could have on the one hand technical experts - for example, an artillery expert - who would then focus on the technical aspects that were believed to be relevant for the Trial Chamber. Among the second category of experts, we also had senior officers, former generals, or others who would testify or would be called to testify on their expertise in relation to command and control, and they would only review a minimum of documents in order to support their conclusions because their expertise would be the main basis for their conclusions. So, I mean, the two approaches are complementary and this was applied then and it's my understanding that Mr. Nicholson tries to describe that approach also in his article of 2003. And this is also what I have described in my article of 2009, because I believe that that approach makes a lot of sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I am looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the break, can I ask the assistance of the usher to give a clean copy of the article to Mr. Theunens as he asked for to review during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you are invited to read it and to see to what extent you agree or disagree with. Could Mr. Theunens be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break of 20 minutes. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Could I meanwhile deal with a matter related to Witness Turkusic and Witness Higgs. During their testimonies, D356 and D399 were marked for identification. Now, for D356, which are excerpts of an 82-millimetre mortar menu, the Prosecutor was waiting for a translation of selected additional excerpts, and Chamber wonders whether the translation are there yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could perhaps we hear an answer later this morning. Welcome back, Mr. Theunens. Mr. Ivetic, you amy proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, have you had an opportunity during the break to review the entirety of the article by Mr. Nicholson which I have provided by way of the Court Usher?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find any areas of that article where you are in drastic odds with what is written by Mr. Nicholson that you would like to highlight for us, or do you consider that on the overall you agree with most of what is written there?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would agree to most of what is written based, again, on the fact that this article dates from 2003. And I think Mr. Nicholson had left the ICTY the year before or in the course of 2002, so the situation he was describing, without referring explicitly to the ICTY, but still was, in my view, different to the situation I have known at ICTY, for example, in relation to the availability of what I would call primary sources, i.e., military documentation concerning the parties that the analyst was to -- to -- yeah, to analyse.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to, I believe, the next page in e-court of this article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this touches on an area that you have mentioned about the -- access to documents. Under heading 3, "Evidence Requirements for Military Analysis," Mr. Nicholson writes as follows: "Military analysis, as defined above, demands specific forms of evidence to establish the fullest and most comprehensive picture as possible. It is critical to note that breadth of sources is vital for quality analysis and that the majority of evidence will not come from victim and 'low-level witnesses to crimes' testimony but from information collected by other means." Do you agree with what is written here by Mr. Nicholson?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you feel that for purposes of your work on the report that we have in the Mladic case, which has been identified now as P3029 marked for identification, that you have adhered to this requirement to have a breadth of sources?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I would like to say is as follows, and again I explained that in my previous answer that when Mr. Nicholson drafted his article he was not necessarily familiar with - how would I say it? - the facts that over the years the ICTY, I mean, the OTP, obtained an enormous volume of original documents that had been released or disseminated by the parties themselves, in a sense that -- I mean, I arrived here in July 2009. The OTP had obtained a large volume of documents concerning the Krajina Serbs that originate mainly from archives in Croatia. Since these documents had been seized by the Croatian Armed Forces, i.e., the HV, during Operation Storm, later on, the OTP obtained documents from the authorities of the Republic of Serbia, FRY, Serbia-Montenegro, and so on. There was also an increasing number of archive missions which all allowed to gather original documents concerning the activities, I mean, events, organisations, personalities, activities, analysts were to review, study and prepare conclusions on. So where I agree with the importance of looking at different types of sources, for the specific requirements of an expert report, for example, or a report that could be considered an expert report, my conclusion is that primary documents are the most important source. Obviously, if there is evidence from other sources or information from other sources that would, for example, contradict events or statements or any other information included in these primary documents, i.e., documents by the parties themselves, then those have to be studied too. But otherwise from my experience, these primary documents are the best source and the most effective in order to, yeah, draft an analytical report on the subject matter like the one covered in the underlying report or the report we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just ask a question, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Theunens, Mr. Nicholson gives examples in the next paragraph of the kind of documents that he thinks should be consulted. And without accepting that that is necessarily an exhaustive list, would you agree or disagree with him in principle that the kind of documents he refers to there are similar to the kind of documents that you say are necessary to consult, primary documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do what? Disagree or agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree. I do agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Moloto.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe the Judge's question was in relation to the paragraph on indigenous documents. As I -- I read this article --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the next ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the next one, pardon me, on de jure documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The remain paragraphs in this section identify what comes to a total of six different categories or types of sources that Mr. Nicholson is talking about. Can you look at these categories, sir, and tell us if your report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you -- I think Judge Moloto, and I verified with that, said or meant to say and the next ones, not only the de jure documents but the whole list of documents as we find it under the evidence requirements for military analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perfect. Then I apologise. I stand corrected. And the Judge has anticipated my next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'd like to ask now, in relation to these six types of sources, can you confirm if your report relies on each of these types or if only certain types, if you could identify what types?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ivetic. I'm not sure whether you understand the methodology or what I have tried to answer in the previous -- in my previous answers. It is not a question of looking at all the categories and then ticking the box, and then saying, Yes, I have used all these categories so it has to be a good report. You have to look at the specific requirements and the material that is available to you. I have never used, throughout the -- I think the ten reports I have compiled here, I have never used witness interviews, for example. Why? Not that I have doubts about these witnesses, whether it's Prosecution or Defence witnesses, but the basic question for me was: Well, a witness can say one thing in a statement, but if that witness is not called to provide evidence, then people may doubt about what he said in his statement. Or, and we have seen that, whether it's Defence witnesses or Prosecution witnesses, or witnesses called by these parties, they may say one thing in a statement, they may testify to another thing. So in my view, and again given the ability -- the abundant availability of primary documents, I do not see a requirement to use witness statement. Open source information, I have used that a few times. Why? Because, for example, a public statement of a commanding officer can be quite indicative of, as we discussed last week, his state of mind, his personality. If it is about certain events, from the methodological point of view, I would still try to look for or I still try to identify primary documents because in my view they are, generally speaking, more reliable sources that open sources. But it's not a black and white situation. You look at it, and you apply the methodology case-by-case. Internationals? Of course. I have seen many documents both when I was working in peacekeeping missions as well as when I was here, for example, of meetings between internationals and certain military officials, or reports on the situation, I mean, drawn by these international organisations. And there again, I may have used some of those, but I will always like to look for the primary documents in order to find corroboration. Intelligence. This is one of the issues where I have problem with the article. Mr. Nicholson uses the expression "intelligence" without defining it. There is a lot of confusion and mystery about intelligence. Intelligence is not espionage. Intelligence simply is information that has been subjected to most often human judgement. So that is the difference between intelligence and -- between information and intelligence. Sorry, I will repeat. And I'm sorry I'm a bit fast. Intelligence is not to be confused with espionage. Everybody does intelligence. It is just subjecting information to your human judgement in the framework of specific requirements you have. Looking at the types of intelligence Mr. Nicholson lists, imagery, I have not used that; human intelligence, I have not used that; signals intercepts, I didn't use those, because again I felt that the primary documents that were available to me were sufficient in order to draw the kind of report I -- to draft the kind of report I have drafted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please turn to page 8 of this document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have just one more item I would like to address with you. It is under the heading of "Strategic Use of the Broader Analysis Function," and is the fourth paragraph down from the top of that section. And it reads as follows: "The analyst should have a separated management chain in terms of the execution of his/her professional obligations to the OTP, namely objectivity, ethical analyse process, qualitative contribution, and proper utilisation of the resource." First of all, sir, do you agree with the position expressed herein on this topic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I should see the context in which Mr. Nicholson drafted this paragraph because I haven't cited from it. I think I understand why he wrote it, but I am not sure, so, I mean -- obviously, an analyst has to be able to apply the methodology in the most independent possible manner without being influenced by outside factors. We are all biassed. You're biassed, I'm biassed, we're all biassed. But a good analyst will be able to identify bias and also to prevent it in expressing or in applying, I'm sorry, the methodology. So that -- I don't think I can say more about this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you then about your own work, sir. Do you feel that as a part of your work within the MAT and for purposes of the expert reports you have authored for cases including this one, do you feel that you had a separate management chain?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it's not so much a management chain. You know, I was given a dead-line by -- first of all, in general, when I was still working here, the trial team asked me or my team leader, rather, whether I could draft a report. In the affirmative case, there was a conversation about the subject matter, so I asked for guidelines as well as for a dead-line. And then it was basically up to me to draft a report within the set dead-lines. There were no outside influence as to what I was about to write or which documents I was about to consult. And then when the dead-line approached I submitted a draft report. There may be a meeting on it in order to clarify certain issues. But otherwise, the report would be -- we called it the in-house databases. And then you have based on, I mean, the ongoing trial and calendar and so on, I would be called to testify or not. This is in a nutshell the management process that existed when I was still working at the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the document as the next available Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1496 receives number D447, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Absence of any objections, admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to 65 ter number 1D1492 in e-court. And if we could turn to page 3 of the same in e-court. That should correlate to the transcript page 4399 of the Hadzic proceedings. And I would like to focus on lines 4 through 15 of the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I will read this and ask some comments from you following. So please follow along: "Q. And who was signing your e-passes over the course of the eight years that you were employed by the Tribunal? "A. My -- I mean, the first reporting officers I mentioned earlier, those were the team leaders of the military analysis team, and then the second reporting officer I believe it was in most cases Mr. Bob Reid and I forget now the official job title he had -- but I mean he was a senior investigator and then I think he -- whether he was a chief of investigations or -- I think he was chief of investigations for most of the time. "Q. In any event, he's a part of the Office of the Prosecutor; is that right? "A. That is correct, yeah." Sir, is this testimony from the Hadzic trial truthful and accurate such that you would testify the same way today if asked these question subject to the solemn declaration you have taken?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain for us or for those unfamiliar with the system what is an e-pass and what is its significance within the management chain?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, e-pass stands for electronic appraisal system which is the common system for UN staff members for their annual appraisal, performance appraisal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the e-pass a source for -- or a source document that is to be submitted for future employment opportunities that are applied through the UN system?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually it is and then the applicant is invited to submit his or her last two e-passes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you consider Bob Reid to have been from a separate management chain in the spirit of the Mr. Nicholson's article that we have just looked at?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn back one page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you said Mr. Bob Reid was from a separate management chain, where does Mr. Nicholson say in his article that a human being forms part of a management chain? The paragraph that you read out to Mr. Theunens just before you removed the last document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The paragraph from Mr. Nicholson's article says: "The analyst should have a separate management chain in terms of the execution of his/her professional obligations to the OTP," and it talks about objectivity, et cetera. Perhaps I should ask the witness, is his understanding of the separate chain meaning someone who is not involved in the Prosecutor and the investigations of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. My problem is if you read that paragraph by Mr. Nicholson, it doesn't mention a human being as part of that chain. It talks of objectivity, professional something, something, and two other things: Proper use of his sources and ethical -- and analytical ethics. There is no mention of a human being forming that separate chain, management chain. Now Mr. Bob Reid is a human being. He's neither of the four things that are mentioned by Mr. Nicholson.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And perhaps if we could briefly go back to that document which has now been marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: D447, thank you, Your Honour. And if we could go to page 9 of the same. This is the continuation of the Nicholson article. And at the top there is talk of structure under heading 9, and it says: "The analyst should support the investigative function and investigative teams from outside of the immediate investigative management structure. This ensures integrity of tasking, quality of product, focus of requirements, and proper use of resources. Similarly, the analyst should support the Prosecution's team from without but working in close liaison with attorneys to provide advice, knowledge, and guidance of the case."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You accept that this is something --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do, Your Honours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this doesn't talk about management chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the context of this part of Mr. Nicholson's article, do you consider that having Mr. Bob Reid as one of the persons responsible for your e-pass is consistent with the analyst, you, being from outside of the immediate investigative management structure?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mean, I'm not sure whether it is an effective use of court time to explain the electronic UN appraisal system, but -- or maybe you should review my -- the e-passes I had from the ICTY. The first reporting officer was my team leader in the military analysis team, while I was mainly working with trial teams. So from that point of view, there is a separate management chain, because I worked together with investigators, trial attorneys, senior trial attorneys, but they don't write my e-pass. They are not my first reporting officer. My team leader in the military analysis team was my first reporting officer. The second reporting officer, indeed, was a person of the -- of the same management chain, but, again, if you're familiar with this system, a second reporting officer rarely writes something else or rarely amends what the first reporting officer has said because Mr. Reid, I think there were several hundreds of staff for whom he was the second reporting officer, it would have been difficult for him I think, just from a human point of view, to have a detailed views on the work performance of each and every of these several hundred staff members. I don't recall exactly what Mr. Reid may have written in my previous e-passes, but again I repeat myself, I'm sorry for that, the first reporting officer was the team leader of the MAT. So from that point of view, the requirement as you describe it is indeed met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We may just clarify this point again, and I know that the e-pass system is not part of this case. Your first reporting officer would have been your direct supervisor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And your second reporting officer is not necessarily the person who works with you on a daily basis but he may be at the head of the section which you are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does he form a membership of the immediate management structure within which you work, given that situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it would be unusual for him or her to address me directly as a second reporting officer. It would make more sense to go by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Would you see him as forming part of your immediate management structure if he is somebody up there and not working with you on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now return to 65 ter number 1D1492. And this time turn to page 2 of the same. And this will correlate to transcript page 4397. It will be at the bottom of page, starting at lines 20 through 25, and will bleed over onto lines 1 through 10 of the next page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, sir, if you could follow along as I read into the record what is reflected and then I will have some follow-up questions: "Q. And in assessing command and control structures, organisations, roles of the military, in a given week how often did you speak, exchange an e-mail, pick up the telephone and speak with lawyers in the Office of the Prosecutor during your eight years with the Tribunal? "A. Your Honours, I wasn't requested to keep statistics. I don't want to give the impression that I want to argue, but one of your colleagues once asked me how my salary was established. I think it was in the Vukovar case, whether I was paid -- "Q. Mr. Theunens -- "A. -- whether I was paid in according to the results that were achieved. Of course I had daily contacts with other team members and those team members consisted of lawyers, I mean senior trial attorneys, trial attorneys, junior lawyers, interns, as I had contacts with investigators and criminal analysts. "Q. So the answer to my question is daily? "A. Yes." First of all, sir, can you confirm that this is all accurate and truthful such that you would stand by the same today if asked the same questions subject to the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours. I confirm that this is an accurate reflection of my testimony. And if I would -- you would ask me the same, I may leave out the reference to the Vukovar case because it's maybe not relevant. But otherwise, I would say the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to the contact that you would have had on a daily basis with various members of the Office of the Prosecution as outlined herein, did you ever have occasion to participate in meetings or offer advice about the drafting or amendment of indictments?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to ask for clarification because I'm a bit confused. Are you asking for this case and this report or are you asking for everything that happened prior to the drafting of this report?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My use of the term "did you ever" implies both A and B of your two scenarios, both before and including this case.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I left the ICTY in April 2009, so after that I had no meetings with any members of the OTP except in relation to drafting expert reports or reports after that date, and those I think were Hadzic and Mladic. Those two cases. As for before 2009, I indeed participated in meetings concerning the review of indictments. But as I have testified in other trials, my input was limited to ensuring that the appropriate or the accurate military terminology was being used when military events, personalities, positions, and so on were being discussed or were being addressed in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could return to 1D1498. And if we could turn to page 6 of the same in e-court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once we get to page 6, I would like to together look at -- together look at second paragraph under the heading "Role of Militarily Expertise During the Investigative Phase": "(Military) analysts apply a methodology which is commonly known as the 'intelligence cycle.' The intelligence cycle consists of four discrete phases: Direction, collection, processing, dissemination. Based on the direction received from the Senior Trial attorneys, the analyst will participate in the collection of information. The analyst's specialist knowledge can assist in better focussing the direction and the collection." Does this -- does this paragraph accurately describe the situation you operated under for purposes of drafting your various expert reports while at the MAT at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, Your Honours, because, for example, in -- in context of the Vukovar case, I mean, Mrksic, Sljivancanin, Radic, the trial attorney -- I asked -- I mean, the trial attorney clearly told me -- the Senior Trial Attorney clearly told me, I want to have a report on the role of these three individuals as well as on the role of Operational Group South. And then we would have a discussion as to, Okay, when would you like to start with the report, i.e., what would be the starting date or the time-period I was to cover, what would be the end date. So that is the nature of the direction that was given by the Senior Trial Attorney.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could look at footnote number 16 from this selection. It's at the bottom of the page. Perhaps you can zoom in on it some more as it is smaller in size. You identify, "The intelligence cycle is universally applied in the implementation of the process of intelligence." I want to ask you, sir, is it your position that the intelligence cycle is the only accepted methodology for the processing of intelligence?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't understand the question because what do you mean by "the process of intelligence"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The processing of intelligence. I apologise if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I understand it processing is a phase of the intelligence cycle which consists of evaluation, colation, analysis, integration, and interpretation. So if you have another definition for processing, then maybe I am in a better position to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me what definition you meant what you used the word "process of intelligence" in footnote 16.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the -- I mean, as it is stated there and as I have given, the intelligence cycle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What -- I mean, I'm trying to understand your question. I may well be that you are referring to other terminology to identify the phases of the intelligence cycle. I know that criminal analysts, for example, they don't like to -- or they don't use direction, they have consultation or something for the first phase. And I've also seen some more recent US doctrinal publications that kind of split or divide the processing phase in a different manner. But otherwise I stick to the intelligence cycle as I have given it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it your position that within the community of analysts, the intelligence cycle methodology has not been the subject of criticism for flaws?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with -- I mean, there are lots of discussions, and especially with the internet and blogs where, I mean, people can basically publish what they want. There is a lot of debate, but it doesn't put into question this methodology; otherwise, you should put some specific challenges to me and give me the opportunity to comment on them. I am not inclined to put the methodology into question because you say that there are a few people that have -- have put it into question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you consider the publishers Routledge to be bloggers or internet columnists?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. And, you know -- I don't consider them bloggers or internal columnist. But again Routledge publishes I don't know how many -- how many books a day or how many studies, so come with a specific claim and then give me the opportunity to review it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I promise you we'll do that. I'd like to finish with your article first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue. Mr. Theunens, I'm revisiting one of the previous question put to you. That is about intelligence cycle and processing. In the text of the article, a methodology is mentioned commonly known as the intelligence cycle. And then it continues that the intelligence cycle consists of four discrete phases, one of them being processing. Now in the footnote, I read: "The intelligence cycle is universally applied in the implementation of the process of intelligence ..." That confuses me because in the text the processing is described as one of the phases of the intelligence cycle, whereas in the footnote it seems that the intelligence cycle the something is you would apply in the implementation of what is one of the phases of that same intelligence cycle as described in the text. Could you -- apart from definitions, could you explain to me whether this is unfortunate use of language or whether my confusion is based on perhaps a misunderstanding? Could you further explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the use of the expression "processing," paragraph 16, is indeed an unfortunate use of language in the sense that it could also have been there the implementation of the intelligence activities or something like that. I mean, there is always a discussion whether intelligence is a product or a process, but then the word "process" does not mean the same as the processing phase of the intelligence cycle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, did you mean to say footnote 16 instead of paragraph 16?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Yeah. It should be "footnote 16."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So you could say in the implementation of the activity of intelligence or in the implementation of intelligence support as you usually see it in the doctrinal publications to avoid this potential confusion over the expression "process."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there in the footnote, the word "process" is used as covering the four phases of what you call the intelligence cycle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we can turn to page 8 in e-court. And once we get there, I will be interested in footnote number 25. And if we could perhaps zoom in on the footnote, that should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here, sir, you state as follows: "The party that wishes to introduce intercepts into evidence must demonstrate that the recordings are genuine and that the voices that are heard in the recording belong to the persons it alleges. The authentication is achieved through witnesses who testify to the procedures and circumstances of the intercepts and recordings, and witnesses who can identify the voices." Now, sir, in relation to this issue of intercepts, in your opinion would you ascribe a lesser reliability factor to purported intercepts for which there is no corroborative recording but only written notes of what allegedly was heard?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are two aspects: There is the reliability of the source and the credibility of the information, as we explained when discussing the methodology. At face value, if you only have handwritten notes and not the original recording, you would say that the source is less reliable than when you have a real intercept. However, it may well still be that the information in those notes is credible and that you have to see by applying the methodology; i.e., by seeking corroboration, identifying other sources that discuss the same event, and then see whether the information between these different sources or provided by these different sources is consistent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page in e-court. And I'd like to focus on the second paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I propose to go through the -- that one and the two remaining paragraphs on this page and the first sentence on the next page and ask you some questions in relation to this: "Taking into account the complexity of the cases before the ICTY (and other International Tribunals and Courts), it should be obvious that (military) analysis should be placed on equal footing with other components of the investigation. (Military) analysis should be included from the very beginning in all parts of the investigation. It should also be clear that the use of the in-house political, financial, military or other expertise should not be restricted to the analysis of documentary evidence only, but as explained here-above, the in-house expertise also needs to be actively involved in the review of other evidence, as well as the collection of evidence. "Because of their specific knowledge, analysts should also assist with the preparation, or, provided they have received training in this area, participate in the taking of statements of senior witnesses and/or suspects. Experience shows that high level political and military leaders tend to be more co-operative when they are interviewed by people who have a similar educational and/or professional background (i.e. education and training as a military officer), and who are familiar with the events that are discussed. This applies in particular to military witnesses and suspects, who expect OTP staff interviewing them to be familiar with the doctrine of their armed forces, the operations of their units, the background to the conflict, etc. Members of armed forces also appear to be more inclined to share their thoughts with other members of armed forces (even if these are totally different armed forces). "Even though (military) analysts are part of the OTP and work under the direction of senior trial attorneys, it is important to emphasise that the task of a military (or any other) analyst is not simply to assist in building a case against an Accused by selecting only incriminating information. The analyst's role is to review and analyse as much information as possible with the aim of compiling a picture that is as comprehensive and as accurate (i.e. as close to the facts) as possible. The need for accuracy and objectivity is not only a matter of professional ethics, but also one of the requirements to be accepted as an expert witness by a Trial Chamber (see below)." Now, sir, I went through that entire section so as not to myopically view out of context of the words. Does all of this together accurately and truthfully reflect the position that you held at the time that you were part of the MAT and your understanding of the role of an analyst of your type within the OTP?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I still hold these views.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I guess, Your Honours, if we could ask for this document to also be introduced into evidence. We've used it quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, apparently. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1498 receives number D448, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in order to better understand this situation, can you tell us if you have actually participated in interviews of witnesses or suspects while at the OTP. And if so, how many instances in particular for suspects?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did indeed participate in the interviews of military witnesses and suspects, including also some senior political officials. I have no exact recollection of the number of suspects. I think the number was very small.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can focus on the suspects for which you participated in the interviews. During those occasions, did you ever take the lead and directly question the suspects yourself?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember at least one interview, indeed, where I asked a number of questions, clearly supervised by a Senior Trial Attorney who was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you offer advice to other Prosecution staff before, during, or after suspect interviews?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours, and that advice was limited to clarifying what I would call military issues; i.e., if there were any military events that were going to be discussed or military structures or personalities, then the investigative team could ask me for my support or I volunteered this kind of support just to provide that military context to the team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And now I want to focus on witness interviews. I'm not concerned with the number. But during those interviews, did you ever take the lead and directly question witnesses yourself?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I did, and this concerned both witnesses called by the Prosecution as well as witnesses by the Defence. And I would invite you to review the trial records of the trials where these people -- these witnesses testified, and then you will see to what extent these interviews were conducted in a professional manner. I think one good example is the interview that was conducted of retired General Miodrag Panic, who was the chief of staff of the OG South and the Guards Motorised Brigade, and he also testified as a Defence witness in the trial of Colonel Mrksic, Colonel Sljivancanin, and Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have mentioned OG South. I'd like to ask if you have an approximation of how many of the suspect or witness interviews you participated in actually pertained to topics germane to parts of the Mladic indictment?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
